analysis.one_liner: Tightens federal safety rules for gas and hazardous liquid pipelines after a major New Jersey pipeline accident.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee in January 1995 and never received a hearing, vote, or any further action before the 104th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: After a natural gas pipeline explosion in Edison, New Jersey, this bill would have let the Transportation Department bill pipeline companies for the cost of investigating accidents they cause, required companies to run inspection devices through their pipelines and set a schedule for doing so, and required automatic or remote-controlled shutoff valves that work even when power is lost. It also would have required pipeline operators to notify people living within 1,000 yards of a pipeline every year about how to report digging or dumping and what to do in an accident, banned excavation and solid waste dumping in pipeline rights-of-way, and funded state 'one-call' systems that let diggers check for buried pipelines before excavating.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live or work near gas and hazardous liquid pipelines — especially residents within 1,000 yards of an interstate transmission line — get annual notification of the pipeline's location, a phone number for reporting dangerous digging or dumping, and accident procedures [S2][S3]. The public generally benefits from faster shutoff of gas in a rupture, better inspection data, and less excavation damage to pipelines, which is the leading cause of pipeline accidents. Taxpayers benefit because the government can recover up to $500,000 per accident in investigation costs from the responsible company [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Requires regulations for remotely or automatically controlled valves that can shut off gas flow during an accident, including when the primary power source is lost, wherever technically and economically feasible [S3].

Requires pipeline owners and operators to run instrumented internal inspection devices ('smart pigs') through their pipelines to establish baseline safety information, and shortens the deadline for the Secretary to issue inspection regulations from three years to one while requiring an inspection schedule [S2][S3].

Requires annual notification to all residents within 1,000 yards of an interstate pipeline of its location, how to report excavation or dumping, and what to do in an accident, and directs public service announcements on pipeline safety [S2][S3].
Lets the Secretary of Transportation recover up to $500,000 per accident in investigation and oversight costs from companies whose accidents cause death, injury, or more than $250,000 in damage [S3].

Prohibits excavation and solid waste disposal within pipeline rights-of-way and authorizes federal grants to states and one-call notification systems, with the federal share capped at 50 percent, so diggers can check for buried pipelines before excavating [S2][S3].

Directs the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to review how it sites natural gas transmission lines in urban areas, including route selection and right-of-way widths, and makes educational material available to local governments [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Pipeline companies that transport natural gas and hazardous liquids would bear the direct costs: accident investigation cost recovery, mandated inspection runs with smart pigs, installation of remote or automatic shutoff valves, annual resident notification mailings, and penalties for excavation violations in their rights-of-way [S3]. Some of those compliance costs would likely flow through to pipeline customers in rates. The bill authorizes about $100 million in appropriations over three years for pipeline safety programs, funded by taxpayers [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Gas and hazardous liquid pipeline operators

drawbacks.text: The valve requirement applies only 'wherever technically and economically feasible' and the bill instructs the Secretary to give special consideration to pipeline industry recommendations, such as those of the Gas Research Institute — language that could narrow the rule's reach [S3].

Compliance costs for inspections, valves, and notifications would fall on pipeline companies and could be passed on to customers through rates; the one-call grants also require states to spread system costs across underground facility owners rather than fully funding them federally [S3].
Cost recovery is capped at $500,000 per accident and only applies above a $250,000 damage threshold, so taxpayers still absorb much of the cost of investigating major accidents [S3].

The excavation and dumping ban and notification duties impose new compliance burdens on operators and restrict lawful excavation activity near rights-of-way, which could affect landowners and contractors working near pipelines [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets the main causes of pipeline accidents — undetected corrosion or flaws that smart pigs find, third-party excavation damage that one-call systems prevent, and uncontrolled gas release after a rupture that remote valves limit. The compliance costs are real but modest relative to the damage a single urban pipeline rupture causes, as the Edison, New Jersey accident the bill responds to demonstrated. Its weakest points are the industry-friendly escape hatches in the valve provision and the low cost-recovery cap.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee on January 5, 1995, and the committee never took it up — no hearing, no markup, no vote — so it died when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Senator Frank Lautenberg of New Jersey, joined by Senator Bill Bradley, introduced the bill on January 5, 1995 in response to the Edison, New Jersey natural gas pipeline accident [S1][S3][S5].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day [S5].
No further action appears in the bill's record — the committee never held a hearing or vote, and the bill expired with the 104th Congress [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pipeline companies avoided the new inspection, valve, notification, and cost-recovery requirements. Residents near pipelines got no added protection from the federal government, though it did bear the risk of continued accidents.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Pipeline operators, untouched by new rules

sides.party_line_note: Only two Democratic senators from New Jersey were involved and the bill never reached a vote, so no party-line pattern exists in the record.

industries.industry: Natural gas and hazardous liquid pipeline operators
industries.note: The bill would have billed them for accident investigations, required smart-pig inspections and baseline safety data, mandated remote or automatic shutoff valves, and made them notify neighbors annually — real compliance costs, and their interest in avoiding them ran against residents' safety. Its failure left the existing, lighter regulatory regime in place.

The bill banned excavation and solid waste disposal in pipeline rights-of-way and pushed one-call systems that require diggers to check before excavating. That adds friction for contractors but prevents the excavation strikes that endanger workers and neighborhoods.
The bill authorized federal grants, capped at a 50 percent federal share, to establish and promote one-call systems, which are the main defense against diggers accidentally rupturing pipelines.
